claims.evidence: Based on comparison of exosome-mediated delivery (50% increase) versus direct transfection (70-fold increase) shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Similar inefficient exosome-mediated Cas9/gRNA delivery results have been reported elsewhere.
claims.source: Similar experiments were performed using Cas9-enriched exosomes secreted by MDA-MB231 cells, and we found that these exosomes were also inefficient for the Cas9/gRNA delivery to MDA-MB231 cells as a reporter (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F). Our findings were similar to those reported previously (de Jong et al., 2020; Haimovich et al., 2017; Somiya and Kuroda, 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (de Jong et al., 2020; Haimovich et al., 2017; Somiya and Kuroda, 2021) reporting similar findings.

claims.claim: Cas9-GFP from exosomes was internalized into U2OS cells and accumulated in intracellular puncta in ~30% of cells during a 16 hr incubation.
claims.source: Tagged GFP antibody was used to detect internalized Cas9-GFP that accumulated in intracellular puncta in ~30% of the cells during a 16 hr incubation (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1H demonstrating intracellular GFP and CD63 puncta.

claims.claim: Cas9 was internalized into cells but may not have been mobilized from vesicles to gain access to the luciferase reporter genes in the nucleus.
claims.source: From these experiments, we concluded that Cas9 was internalized into cells but may not have been mobilized from vesicles to gain access to the luciferase reporter genes in the nucleus.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that Cas9 was internalized (Figure 1H) but did not result in efficient gene editing (Figure 1F).

claims.claim: Unfractionated conditioned medium from donor cells incubated with reporter cells for 3-8 days showed little change in the Nluc/Fluc signal.
claims.source: Unfractionated conditioned medium from the donor cells was incubated with reporter cells for 3–8 days with little change in the Nluc/Fluc signal (Figure 1I).
claims.evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1I demonstrating minimal signal change with conditioned medium.

claims.claim: Co-culture of donor and acceptor cells in a transwell chamber separated by a 0.45 μm pore membrane for 6 days showed no increase in Nluc/Fluc.
claims.source: As a further test of vesicle stability, we incubated donor and acceptor cells in a transwell chamber separated by a 0.45 μm pore vesicle-permeable membrane. After a 6-day co-culture, no increase in the Nluc/Fluc was observed (Figure 1I).
claims.evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1I demonstrating no signal increase in transwell co-culture.

claims.claim: Delivery of Cas9 is limited by inefficient fusion of exosomes with the endosomal membrane.
claims.source: Therefore, we suggest delivery of Cas9 is limited by inefficient fusion of exosomes with the endosomal membrane (Figure 1J).
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that exosomes are internalized but do not deliver functional Cas9, suggesting a fusion limitation.

claims.claim: Substantial Nluc expression was observed in all donor-acceptor combinations except where HEK293T cells served as both donor and acceptor.
claims.source: After a co-culture for 6 days to near confluence, we observed substantial Nluc expression in all combinations except where HEK293T cells served as both donor and acceptor (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2A demonstrating Nluc expression in various cell combinations.

claims.claim: The highest level of Nluc expression (~60-fold increase in the Nluc/Fluc signal) was seen in co-culture of HEK293T and MDA-MB-231 cells.
claims.source: The highest level of Nluc expression (~60-fold increase in the Nluc/Fluc signal) was seen in co-culture of HEK293T and MDA-MB-231 cells.
claims.evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2A demonstrating highest signal with HEK293T-MDA-MB-231 co-culture.

claims.claim: There was little difference in the efficiency of transfer with CD63-tethered or free Cas9/gRNA.
claims.source: Of note, we found little difference in the efficiency of transfer with CD63-tethered or free Cas9/gRNA.
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison of different Cas9 constructs in Figure 2A showing similar transfer efficiency.

claims.claim: Progressive transfer was observed over several days with a limit reached after day 3.
claims.source: In a time-course experiment, we observed progressive transfer over several days with a limit reached after day 3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by time-course data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A demonstrating increasing signal up to day 3.

claims.claim: A gradual increase in signal was observed at higher levels of donor cells, but HEK293T cells serving as both donor and acceptor remained inactive even at a donor:acceptor ratio of 10:1.
claims.source: On increase in the donor:acceptor cell ratio, we observed a gradual increase in the signal at a higher level of donor cell but HEK293T cells serving as both donor and acceptor remained inactive even at a donor:acceptor ratio of 10:1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
claims.evidence: Supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C demonstrating ratio-dependent increase except for HEK293T-HEK293T pairs.

claims.claim: After co-culture of HEK293T and MDA-MB-231 cells, double-positive cells were found indicating transfer of GFP fragments between cells.
claims.source: After co-culture, doubl- positive cells were found (Figure 2C, bottom panel, Q2 and Q2-4 quadrants), suggesting transfer of one or both fragments of GFP between cells (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C demonstrating cells with both GFP and mCherry or CFP signals.

claims.claim: Transfer of GFP11 from HEK293T to MDA-MB-231 occurred in around 6% of cells.
claims.source: GFP+mCherry+/mCherry+ (Figure 2C, bottom panel) represented the ratio of cells with GFP+mCherry double-positive fluorescence, indicating a transfer of GFP11 from HEK293T to MDA-MB-231 in around 6% of cells (Figure 2D and E, yellow bars).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry quantification shown in Figure 2D and E demonstrating ~6% double-positive cells.

claims.claim: Transfer from MDA-MB-231 to HEK293T occurred in around 0.5% of cells.
claims.source: GFP+CFP+/CFP+ (Figure 2C, bottom panel) represented the ratio of cells with GFP+CFP double-positive fluorescence indicating transfer from MDA-MB-231 to HEK293T in around 0.5% of cells (Figure 2D and E, green bars).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry quantification shown in Figure 2D and E demonstrating ~0.5% double-positive cells.

claims.claim: No cargo transfer was seen when HEK293T cells served as both donor and acceptor.
claims.source: As a control, HEK293T cells expressing CFP and CD63 fused 7*tandem GFP11 (Figure 2C, top panel) were co-cultured with HEK293T cells expressing mCherry and GFP1-10 (Figure 2F, top panel, P3 area). No cargo transfer was seen in this combination (Figure 2F, bottom panel, Q2 and Q2-4 quadrants).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2F demonstrating absence of double-positive cells in Q2 and Q2-4 quadrants.

claims.claim: Co-cultures of MDA-MB-231 as donor to several other tumor cell lines as acceptor (ratio of 10:1) resulted in cargo transfer to a limit of about 10% of cells.
claims.source: Co-cultures of MDA-MB-231 as the donor to several other tumor cell lines as acceptor (ratio of 10:1) resulted in cargo transfer to a limit of about 10% of cells (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2G demonstrating up to ~10% transfer to various tumor cell lines.

claims.claim: Cargos were transferred from MDA-MB-231 to other cell lines, including the MDA-MB-231 cell line itself.
claims.source: Of note, cargos were also transferred from MDA-MB-231 to other cell lines, including the MDA-MB-231 cell line itself (GFP+CFP+/CFP+ bars in Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2G demonstrating transfer among MDA-MB-231 cells.

claims.claim: Only 0.02% of acceptor cells reported GFP in the 12-24 hr incubation with exosomes, compared to ~6% in co-culture.
claims.source: In contrast to the ~6% of cells that received GFP11 from donor cells in a 3–4-day co-culture, only 0.02% of acceptor cells reported GFP in the 12–24 hr incubation with exosomes (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison of flow cytometry data showing dramatic difference between exosome treatment and co-culture.

claims.claim: Delivery of exosome content may be limited by inefficient fusion to the endosomal membrane for exosomes produced by HEK293T and internalized by MDA-MB-231 cells.
claims.source: These results reinforce the suggestion that the delivery of exosome content may be limited by inefficient fusion to the endosomal membrane at least for exosomes produced by HEK293T and internalized by MDA-MB-231 cells.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that exosomes are internalized but deliver cargo very inefficiently (0.02% vs 6%).

claims.claim: Chlorpromazine, LY294002, and wortmannin did not interfere with Cas9 transfer at concentrations where internalization of transferrin or zymosan was blocked.
claims.source: Chlorpromazine, LY294002, and wortmannin were found not to interfere with Cas9 transfer at concentrations where the internalization of a fluorescently tagged transferrin or zymosan was blocked (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D).
claims.evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 3A showing no effect on Cas9 transfer and imaging data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-D showing blocked endocytosis.

claims.claim: siRNA knockdown of clathrin heavy chain and AP-2 subunit B1 blocked endocytosis but had only a slight effect on Cas9 transfer.
claims.source: Furthermore, siRNA knockdown of clathrin heavy chain and AP-2 subunit B1 (validations in Figure 3—figure supplement 2) blocked endocytosis but had only a slight effect on Cas9 transfer compared to a control (Figure 3B) that dramatically blocked the uptake of transferrin by recipient cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F).
claims.evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 3B showing minimal effect on Cas9 transfer and imaging data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-F showing blocked transferrin uptake.

claims.claim: siRNA knockdown of caveolin and flotillin 2 had little effect on endocytosis of transferrin but stimulated transfer of Cas9.
claims.source: For comparison, we also used siRNA to knockdown caveolin and flotillin 2 with little effect on endocytosis of transferrin but which stimulated transfer of Cas9 (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F).
claims.evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 3B showing increased Cas9 transfer and imaging data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-F showing minimal effect on transferrin uptake.

claims.claim: Endocytosis is not necessary for Cas9/gRNA transfer.
claims.source: Endocytosis, at least as revealed by these particular drug sensitivities and coat protein requirements, appeared not to be necessary for Cas9/gRNA transfer.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that endocytosis inhibitors and knockdowns did not block Cas9 transfer (Figure 3A-B).

claims.claim: Latrunculin A (80 or 200 nM) and Latrunculin B (2.5 or 5 µM) substantially blocked the transfer of Cas9.
claims.source: Lat A (80 or 200 nM) and LatB (2.5 or 5 µM) substantially blocked the transfer of Cas9 (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3C demonstrating dramatic reduction in Cas9 transfer with latrunculin treatment.

claims.claim: Actin shRNA knockdown in donor HEK293T cells reduced Cas9 transfer threefold.
claims.source: Actin shRNA knockdown in donor HEK293T cells reduced Cas9 transfer threefold but was more effective in blocking transfer in acceptor MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 3D and E), which may be because the actin knockdown efficiency was greater in MDA-MB-231 than in HEK293T cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E and H).
claims.evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3D and E demonstrating reduced transfer with actin knockdown.

claims.claim: Actin shRNA knockdown was more effective in blocking transfer in acceptor MDA-MB-231 cells than in donor HEK293T cells.
claims.source: Actin shRNA knockdown in donor HEK293T cells reduced Cas9 transfer threefold but was more effective in blocking transfer in acceptor MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 3D and E), which may be because the actin knockdown efficiency was greater in MDA-MB-231 than in HEK293T cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E and H).
claims.evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3D and E and knockdown validation in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E and H.

claims.claim: Arp2/3 complex knockdown in donor but not in recipient cells reduced Cas9 transfer.
claims.source: Arp2/3 complex knockdown in donor but not in recipient cells reduced Cas9 transfer (Figure 3D and E).
claims.evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3D and E demonstrating differential effects of Arp2/3 knockdown in donor vs recipient cells.

claims.claim: The formin inhibitor SMIFH2 decreased Cas9 transfer dramatically.
claims.source: The formin inhibitor SMIFH2 decreased Cas9 transfer dramatically (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3F demonstrating dramatic reduction in Cas9 transfer with SMIFH2 treatment.

claims.claim: The transfer of Cas9 protein from HEK293T to MDA-MB-231 depends upon actin.
claims.source: These results suggested the transfer of Cas9 protein from HEK293T to MDA-MB-231 depends upon actin and to some extent on the Arp2/3 complex or formin possibly to stabilize a cellular structure essential for intercellular traffic.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that actin depolymerization and knockdown blocked Cas9 transfer (Figure 3C-E).

claims.claim: The transfer of Cas9 protein from HEK293T to MDA-MB-231 depends to some extent on the Arp2/3 complex or formin.
claims.source: These results suggested the transfer of Cas9 protein from HEK293T to MDA-MB-231 depends upon actin and to some extent on the Arp2/3 complex or formin possibly to stabilize a cellular structure essential for intercellular traffic.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that Arp2/3 knockdown and formin inhibition reduced Cas9 transfer (Figure 3D-F).

claims.claim: Membrane tubes appearing as pseudopodia or filopodia projected from HEK293T cells made contact with MDA-MB-231 cells forming open-ended connections.
claims.source: Membrane tubes appearing as pseudopodia or filopodia projected from HEK293T cells were seen to make contact with MDA-MB-231 cells forming what appeared to be open-ended connections (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 4A demonstrating tubular structures connecting cells.

claims.claim: Puncta containing endosome-related vesicles and SBP-Cas9-GFP were transported from HEK293T to MDA-MB-231 cells.
claims.source: On prolonged inspection, puncta containing endosome-related vesicles (labeled with streptavidin-CD63-mCherry) and SBP-Cas9-GFP were transported from HEK293T to MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 4B), consistent with open-ended tubular connections associated with intercellular traffic.
claims.evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 4B demonstrating movement of fluorescent puncta through tubular connections.

claims.claim: Tubular structures formed and broke during the course of visualization.
claims.source: Such structures were seen to form and break during the course of visualization (Figure 4—video 1); however, in spite of a membrane fusion event, we did not observe wholesale cell fusion to form heterokaryons.
claims.evidence: Supported by time-lapse video (Figure 4—video 1) showing dynamic formation and breaking of tubular connections.

claims.claim: Wholesale cell fusion to form heterokaryons was not observed despite membrane fusion events.
claims.source: Such structures were seen to form and break during the course of visualization (Figure 4—video 1); however, in spite of a membrane fusion event, we did not observe wholesale cell fusion to form heterokaryons.
claims.evidence: Based on observation during live-cell imaging that cells remained separate despite tubular connections.

claims.claim: Many thin projections termed tunneling nanotubes formed between neighboring cells.
claims.source: At the same time, many much thinner projections, termed tunneling nanotubes, formed between neighboring cells.
claims.evidence: Based on observation during live-cell imaging of thin tubular structures in addition to thicker connections.

claims.claim: Open-ended tubular connections between HEK293T and MDA-MB-231 cells were confirmed using z-stack imaging and 3D tomography.
claims.source: The open-ended tubular connections were also observed using z-stack imaging and 3D tomography (Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—videos 1 and 2), confirming the observation of open-ended tubular connections between HEK293T and MDA-MB-231 cells.
claims.evidence: Supported by 3D imaging data shown in Figure 5A and B demonstrating open-ended connections from multiple angles.

claims.claim: Serial EM images revealed a potential point of fusion and diverse organelles populating the junction between HEK293T and MDA-MB-231 cells.
claims.source: Serial images were stacked to reveal entire tubular connections between HEK293T and MDA-MB-231 cells (one example in Figure 5E). A trace of the plasma membranes in connecting cells revealed a potential point of fusion and diverse organelles populating the junction between cells.
claims.evidence: Supported by CLEM data shown in Figure 5E demonstrating membrane continuity and organelles at cell junctions.

claims.claim: Cell junctions that appeared to convey cargo were 2 to 4 microns in diameter.
claims.source: The cell junctions that appeared to convey cargo in these cell pairs were much thicker, from 2 to 4 microns in diameter, than the 100–200 nanometer TNTs also seen in our mixed cultures.
claims.evidence: Based on measurement of tubular structures in EM images (Figure 5E).

claims.claim: 8 open-ended tubular connections were found in 120 tubule-cell contacts between HEK293T and MDA-MB-231 cells.
claims.source: Combining the live-cell imaging and CLEM results, we found 8 open-ended tubular connections in 120 tubule-cell contacts, similar to the ratio of recipient cells containing GFP signal after co-culture in the split-GFP assays (Figure 2D and E).
claims.evidence: Based on quantification of open-ended connections observed by live-cell imaging and CLEM.

claims.claim: The ratio of open-ended connections (8 in 120) was similar to the ratio of recipient cells containing GFP signal after co-culture in the split-GFP assays.
claims.source: Combining the live-cell imaging and CLEM results, we found 8 open-ended tubular connections in 120 tubule-cell contacts, similar to the ratio of recipient cells containing GFP signal after co-culture in the split-GFP assays (Figure 2D and E).
claims.evidence: Based on comparison of structural observations with functional transfer data from Figure 2D and E.

claims.claim: No intercellular movement of Cas9 or GFP reporter fragments was seen in cultures of HEK293T donor and acceptor pairs.
claims.source: Although membrane tubules were seen to emanate from HEK293T cells (Figure 4, Figure 4—video 1), no intercellular movement of Cas9 or GFP reporter fragments were seen in cultures of HEK293T donor and acceptor pairs (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Based on luciferase and flow cytometry data in Figure 2 showing no transfer between HEK293T cells.

claims.claim: Tubular connections were observed between HEK293T cells, but no evidence of cytoplasmic continuity was observed.
claims.source: Tubular connections were observed and in cases where the connections remained intact, no evidence of cytoplasmic continuity was observed (Figure 6A, Figure 6—video 1), consistent with our failure to detect Cas9 transfer between cells in a culture of HEK293T.
claims.evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 6A demonstrating tubular connections without cargo transfer.

claims.claim: CLEM revealed a close-ended tubular contact between HEK293T cells.
claims.source: Next, we evaluated HEK293 donor:acceptor cell pairs by CLEM. One such example revealed a close-ended tubular contact (Figure 6B–D), suggesting a failure in plasma membrane fusion at the tubular junction between HEK293T cells.
claims.evidence: Supported by CLEM data shown in Figure 6B-D demonstrating lack of membrane continuity at tubular junctions.

claims.claim: No open-ended tubular connections were found in 120 tubule-cell contacts among HEK293T cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, combining live-cell imaging and CLEM results, we found no open-ended tubular connections in 120 tubule-cell contacts among HEK293T cells.
claims.evidence: Based on quantification of tubular connections observed by live-cell imaging and CLEM in HEK293T-HEK293T co-cultures.

claims.claim: Cargos were transferred through open-ended tubular connections that depend upon a plasma membrane fusion process.
claims.source: Altogether, the above results demonstrated that cargos were transferred through open-ended tubular connections that would depend upon a plasma membrane fusion process where a fusogen catalyst may be contributed by the donor or acceptor plasma membrane.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that open-ended connections correlate with cargo transfer while close-ended connections do not.

claims.claim: Syncytin-1 and syncytin-2 are endogenous retroviral envelope glycoproteins in humans.
claims.source: Two examples are myomaker and myomerger for myoblast fusion, and the syncytins for trophoblast cell fusion (reviewed in Brukman et al., 2019). Syncytins are endogenous retroviral envelope glycoproteins: syncytin-1 and syncytin-2 in humans (Blaise et al., 2003; Frendo et al., 2003; Mi et al., 2000) and syncytin-A and -B in mice (Dupressoir et al., 2005; Peng et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Blaise et al., 2003; Frendo et al., 2003; Mi et al., 2000) establishing syncytins as retroviral envelope proteins.

claims.claim: Syncytin-A and syncytin-B are endogenous retroviral envelope glycoproteins in mice.
claims.source: Syncytins are endogenous retroviral envelope glycoproteins: syncytin-1 and syncytin-2 in humans (Blaise et al., 2003; Frendo et al., 2003; Mi et al., 2000) and syncytin-A and -B in mice (Dupressoir et al., 2005; Peng et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Dupressoir et al., 2005; Peng et al., 2007) establishing mouse syncytins.

claims.claim: ASCT-2 is a receptor for syncytin-1.
claims.source: Syncytin-mediated fusion requires complementary cell surface receptors, including ASCT-2, a widely distributed neutral amino acid transporter, a receptor for syncytin-1 (Blond et al., 2000) and Major Facilitator Superfamily Domain Containing-2 (MFSD2), a sodium-dependent lysophosphatidylcholine transporter, the receptor for syncytin-2 (Esnault et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Blond et al., 2000) identifying ASCT-2 as syncytin-1 receptor.

claims.claim: MFSD2 is a receptor for syncytin-2.
claims.source: Syncytin-mediated fusion requires complementary cell surface receptors, including ASCT-2, a widely distributed neutral amino acid transporter, a receptor for syncytin-1 (Blond et al., 2000) and Major Facilitator Superfamily Domain Containing-2 (MFSD2), a sodium-dependent lysophosphatidylcholine transporter, the receptor for syncytin-2 (Esnault et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Esnault et al., 2008) identifying MFSD2 as syncytin-2 receptor.

claims.claim: Ly6e is a receptor for syncytin-A in mice.
claims.source: In the mouse, lymphocyte antigen 6E (Ly6e) has been identified as a receptor for syncytin-A (Bacquin et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Bacquin et al., 2017) identifying Ly6e as syncytin-A receptor.

claims.claim: Syncytins are involved in the fusion of osteoclast precursors and cancer cells.
claims.source: In addition to a role in the formation of a trophoblast syncytium during early embryonic development, syncytins are also involved in the fusion of osteoclast precursors and cancer cells (Bjerregaard et al., 2006; Uygur et al., 2019a).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Bjerregaard et al., 2006; Uygur et al., 2019a) demonstrating syncytin roles in osteoclast and cancer cell fusion.

claims.claim: The expression of syncytin-1 and syncytin-2 was detected in all tested cell lines.
claims.source: First, we used immunoblotting to detect syncytins in the cell lines used in this study (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A). The expression of syncytin-1 and syncytin-2 was detected in all these lines but the higher mobility, presumably furin processed form of syncytin-2, was more apparent than that of syncytin-1.
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A demonstrating syncytin expression in multiple cell lines.

claims.claim: The higher mobility, presumably furin processed form of syncytin-2, was more apparent than that of syncytin-1.
claims.source: The expression of syncytin-1 and syncytin-2 was detected in all these lines but the higher mobility, presumably furin processed form of syncytin-2, was more apparent than that of syncytin-1.
claims.evidence: Based on observation of protein mobility patterns in immunoblots (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).

claims.claim: MDA-MB-231 cells had a lower level of syncytin-1.
claims.source: MDA-MB-231 cells had a lower level of syncytin-1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A demonstrating reduced syncytin-1 signal in MDA-MB-231 cells.

claims.claim: Knockdown of syncytin-1 in MDA-MB-231 cells partially decreased Cas9 transfer.
claims.source: Knockdown of syncytin-1 in MDA-MB-231 cells partially decreased Cas9 transfer; however, knockdown of syncytin-2 in MDA-MB-231 cells had a greater effect on Cas9 transfer (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–E, lane 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 7A demonstrating reduced transfer with syncytin-1 knockdown.

claims.claim: Knockdown of syncytin-2 in MDA-MB-231 cells had a greater effect on Cas9 transfer than syncytin-1 knockdown.
claims.source: Knockdown of syncytin-1 in MDA-MB-231 cells partially decreased Cas9 transfer; however, knockdown of syncytin-2 in MDA-MB-231 cells had a greater effect on Cas9 transfer (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–E, lane 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 7A demonstrating greater reduction in transfer with syncytin-2 knockdown.

claims.claim: Expression of mouse syncytin-A partially restored Cas9 transfer in syncytin-1 and syncytin-2 knockdowns.
claims.source: Expression of the mouse syncytin, syncytin-A, partially restored Cas9 transfer in the syncytin-1 and syncytin-2 knockdowns (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 7A demonstrating rescue of transfer by syncytin-A expression.

claims.claim: Full-length syncytin-A restored Cas9 transfer, but no truncated versions did.
claims.source: As before, functional restoration of Cas9 transfer was observed by expression of full-length syncytin-A, but no significant Cas9 transfer was observed on expression of any of the syncytin-A truncated versions (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 7C demonstrating rescue only with full-length syncytin-A.

claims.claim: Expression of truncated syncytin-As reduced functional Cas9 transfer below the level achieved by knockdown of syncytin-2 alone.
claims.source: Indeed, expression of truncated syncytin-As reduced functional Cas9 transfer below the level achieved by knockdown of syncytin-2 alone (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 7C demonstrating dominant-negative effect of truncated syncytin-A.

claims.claim: Depletion of syncytin-1 or syncytin-2 in HEK293T cells reduced functional Cas9 transfer by ~30%.
claims.source: Next, we evaluated the effect of syncytin knockdown in HEK293T cells and found that the depletion of syncytin-1 or 2 in HEK293T reduced functional Cas9 transfer by ~30%, a much smaller effect than seen in depletion of syncytin-2 in MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1G and H).
claims.evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 7D demonstrating modest reduction in transfer with syncytin knockdown in HEK293T.

claims.claim: The effect of syncytin depletion in HEK293T cells was much smaller than the effect of syncytin-2 depletion in MDA-MB-231 cells.
claims.source: Next, we evaluated the effect of syncytin knockdown in HEK293T cells and found that the depletion of syncytin-1 or 2 in HEK293T reduced functional Cas9 transfer by ~30%, a much smaller effect than seen in depletion of syncytin-2 in MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1G and H).
claims.evidence: Based on comparison of luciferase assay data in Figure 7A and Figure 7D showing differential effects in different cell types.

claims.claim: Expression of syncytin-A in HEK293T cells serving as a reporter permitted some transfer of Cas9 from HEK293T donor cells.
claims.source: The expression of syncytin-A in HEK293T cells serving as a reporter permitted some transfer of Cas9 from HEK293T cells serving as a donor (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 7E demonstrating increased transfer with syncytin-A expression in HEK293T acceptor cells.

claims.claim: The effect of syncytin-A expression in HEK293T acceptor cells was much less pronounced than when MDA-MB-231 served as acceptor cells (up to 4-fold vs. 30-fold change).
claims.source: Although the effect was much less pronounced than when MDA-MB-231 served as acceptor cells (up to 4-fold vs. 30-fold change of Nluc/Fluc signal indicating Cas9 transfer), this result suggested that functional syncytin may be limited in HEK293T cells, thus explaining the appearance of close-ended tubular connections between HEK293T cells (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: Based on comparison of luciferase assay data showing different magnitudes of transfer enhancement.

claims.claim: Functional syncytin may be limited in HEK293T cells, explaining the appearance of close-ended tubular connections between HEK293T cells.
claims.source: Although the effect was much less pronounced than when MDA-MB-231 served as acceptor cells (up to 4-fold vs. 30-fold change of Nluc/Fluc signal indicating Cas9 transfer), this result suggested that functional syncytin may be limited in HEK293T cells, thus explaining the appearance of close-ended tubular connections between HEK293T cells (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that HEK293T cells form close-ended connections and have limited syncytin function.

claims.claim: Close-ended tubular connections were observed between HEK293T cells and MDA-MB-231 syncytin-2 knockdown cells even after several hours of contact.
claims.source: We visualized HEK293T cells containing SBP-Cas9-GFP and Myc-streptavidin-CD63-mCherry co-cultured with MDA-MB-231 syncytin-2 knockdown cells containing the Fluc:Nluc:mCherry reporter plasmid and found close-ended tubular connections even after several hours of contact (Figure 8A, Figure 8—video 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 8A demonstrating persistent close-ended connections.

claims.claim: CLEM confirmed the failure of plasma membrane fusion in conditions of syncytin-2 knockdown in MDA-MB-231 cells.
claims.source: Further inspection by CLEM confirmed the failure of plasma membrane fusion in conditions of syncytin-2 knockdown in MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 8B–D).
claims.evidence: Supported by CLEM data shown in Figure 8B-D demonstrating lack of membrane continuity with syncytin-2 knockdown.

claims.claim: Only one open-ended tubular connection was found in 120 tubule-cell contacts of co-cultures using MDA-MB-231 syncytin-2 knockdown cells.
claims.source: In combining live-cell imaging and CLEM results, we found only one open-ended tubular connections in 120 tubule-cell contacts of co-cultures using MDA-MB-231 syncytin-2 knockdown cells.
claims.evidence: Based on quantification of tubular connections observed by live-cell imaging and CLEM with syncytin-2 knockdown.

claims.claim: Syncytin-2 is required or rate-limiting for membrane fusion at the point of contact between a tubule and the other cell plasma membrane.

claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that syncytin-2 knockdown dramatically reduces open-ended connections and cargo transfer.

claims.claim: GFP-tagged syncytin-A, -1, and -2 localized in a reticular pattern within transfected cells with some label detected at or near the cell surface.
claims.source: To further confirm the role of syncytins in membrane fusion at the site of cell-cell contact, we visualized the localization of syncytins by transient transfection of MDA-MB-231 cells with GFP-tagged forms of syncytin-A, -1, and -2. These results showed that most GFP-fusion proteins localized in a reticular pattern within transfected cells with some label detected at or near the cell surface (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–C).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A-C demonstrating intracellular and surface localization.

claims.claim: Cell surface biotinylation detected full-length and furin processed forms of syncytin fusion proteins at the cell surface.
claims.source: Syncytin-fusion proteins were immunoprecipitated with GFP antibody and SDS-PAGE blots were probed with horseradish peroxidase-conjugated streptavidin (streptavidin-HRP) and GFP antibody. HRP blots showed two species that migrated at the positions expected for full-length and furin processed forms of the syncytin fusion proteins (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: Supported by biotinylation assay data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1D demonstrating surface-exposed syncytins.

claims.claim: The majority of syncytin fusion protein molecules accumulated early in the secretory pathway prior to furin cleavage.
claims.source: In contrast, immunoprecipitated fractions blotted with GFP antibody revealed species that migrated at positions expected for the full-length fusion proteins. We interpret this to mean that the majority of molecules accumulated early in the secretory pathway prior to the point of cleavage by the furin protease in the trans-Golgi membrane and beyond.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that GFP blots show primarily full-length protein while biotinylation shows processed forms.

claims.claim: Syncytin-BFP fusions were found partially localized to or near the surface and at junctions between a tubule and the adjoining cell plasma membrane.
claims.source: Next, we visualized HEK293T cells containing SBP-Cas9-GFP and Myc-streptavidin-CD63-mCherry co-cultured with MDA-MB-231 cells containing syncytin 1-BFP (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E) or syncytin 2-BFP (Figure 8—figure supplement 1F). Syncytin-BFP fusions were found partially localized to or near the surface and at junctions between a tubule and the adjoining cell plasma membrane (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E and F).
claims.evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1E and F demonstrating syncytin localization at cell-cell junctions.

claims.claim: Under conditions of transient transfection, some of all three syncytins may be detected at the cell surface and in proximity to sites of membrane fusion.

results.result: Cas9 and gRNA can be enriched in exosomes by tethering Cas9 to CD63 via a streptavidin-biotin binding protein system, and both cargo molecules are sequestered within the exosome lumen.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 demonstrate successful enrichment of Cas9 and gRNA in exosomes using the CD63-tethering strategy, with immunoblot (C1, C3) and qPCR data (C2, C4) showing ~15-fold enrichment. Protease and nuclease protection assays (C5) confirm luminal localization. The experimental design and controls are appropriate.

results.result: Exosome-mediated delivery of Cas9/gRNA is highly inefficient for functional gene editing, despite successful internalization of exosomes into recipient cells, likely due to inefficient fusion of exosomes with endosomal membranes.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C15 and C89 collectively demonstrate that while the reporter system works (C6: 100-fold increase with direct transfection), exosome delivery achieves only 50% increase (C7) versus 70-fold with plasmid (C8). Exosomes are internalized (C11) but fail to deliver functional Cas9 (C12). Transwell and conditioned medium experiments (C13-C14) support the fusion limitation hypothesis (C15). The conclusion is well-supported by converging evidence.

results.result: Cell-cell contact enables highly efficient Cas9/gRNA transfer between co-cultured cells, with HEK293T-MDA-MB-231 pairs showing optimal transfer (~60-fold increase) that is independent of CD63-tethering and increases with time and donor:acceptor ratio.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C20, C90-C91 demonstrate efficient transfer with cell contact using the luciferase reporter system. The data show substantial transfer in most cell combinations except HEK293T-HEK293T (C16, C20), with HEK293T-MDA-MB-231 optimal (C17: ~60-fold). Time-course (C19) and dose-response (C20) data support the robustness of the finding. The lack of CD63-tethering requirement (C18) is an important control.

results.result: A split-GFP assay independently confirms intercellular cargo transfer occurs in ~6% of cells from HEK293T to MDA-MB-231 and ~0.5% in the reverse direction, with no transfer between HEK293T cells, and demonstrates that exosome-mediated transfer is ~300-fold less efficient than cell-cell contact.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C28 provide independent validation using split-GFP. Flow cytometry data (C22-C23) quantify bidirectional transfer with appropriate controls (C24). The comparison of exosome delivery (0.02%, C27) versus co-culture (6%, C22) provides strong quantitative evidence for inefficient exosome fusion (C28). The trifluorescence system elegantly distinguishes donor and acceptor cells.

results.result: Cas9 transfer between cells is independent of clathrin-mediated and caveolin-mediated endocytosis, as demonstrated by pharmacological inhibition and genetic knockdown experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C32 and C93 show that endocytosis inhibitors (chlorpromazine, LY294002, wortmannin) and siRNA knockdowns of endocytic machinery (clathrin, AP-2, caveolin, flotillin 2) do not block Cas9 transfer while effectively blocking transferrin uptake. The controls demonstrating blocked endocytosis are critical and appropriately included. The conclusion that endocytosis is not required (C32) is well-supported.

results.result: Cas9 transfer depends on F-actin and is modulated by actin regulatory proteins (Arp2/3 complex and formin), with latrunculin treatment and actin knockdown substantially blocking transfer.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C39 and C92 demonstrate actin dependence using multiple approaches: latrunculin A/B treatment (C33), actin shRNA knockdown (C34-C35), and inhibition of actin regulators (C36-C37). The differential effects in donor versus acceptor cells (C35-C36) provide mechanistic insight. The data converge on actin-dependent tubular structures as the transfer mechanism (C38-C39).

results.result: Live-cell imaging and correlative light-electron microscopy reveal that cargo transfer occurs through open-ended membrane tubular connections (2-4 μm diameter) between HEK293T and MDA-MB-231 cells, with 8 open-ended connections found in 120 tubule-cell contacts (~6.7%), matching the frequency of functional transfer.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C49 and C94 provide compelling structural evidence for open-ended tubular connections using multiple imaging modalities. Live-cell imaging (C40-C42) shows dynamic tubule formation and cargo movement. CLEM (C45-C46) confirms membrane continuity and organelle presence at junctions. The quantitative correlation (C48-C49) between structural observations (~6.7% open-ended) and functional transfer (~6% by split-GFP) strongly supports the mechanism. The distinction from TNTs (C47) is important.

results.result: HEK293T cells form close-ended tubular connections with each other that are structurally similar to connections with MDA-MB-231 cells but lack cytoplasmic continuity and do not support cargo transfer.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C53 and C95 demonstrate that HEK293T-HEK293T pairs form tubules but lack functional transfer. Live-cell imaging (C51) and CLEM (C52) show close-ended connections without membrane fusion. The quantification (C53: 0/120 open-ended) contrasts sharply with HEK293T-MDA-MB-231 pairs (8/120). This negative control is critical for establishing cell-type specificity of the fusion mechanism.

results.result: Cargo transfer requires open-ended tubular connections formed by plasma membrane fusion, with the fusogen potentially contributed by either donor or acceptor cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C54 synthesizes the structural and functional data to propose a fusion-dependent mechanism. This inference is well-supported by the correlation between open-ended connections and transfer (C48-C49) and the absence of both in HEK293T-HEK293T pairs (C50-C53). The claim appropriately acknowledges that the fusogen source is not yet determined.

results.result: Syncytins are endogenous retroviral envelope glycoproteins that function as fusogens in mammals, with syncytin-1 and syncytin-2 in humans, syncytin-A and -B in mice, and established receptors ASCT-2, MFSD2, and Ly6e.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C60 establish the background knowledge about syncytins through appropriate citations to primary literature. These are well-established facts in the field (Blaise et al., 2003; Mi et al., 2000; Dupressoir et al., 2005; Peng et al., 2007; Blond et al., 2000; Esnault et al., 2008; Bacquin et al., 2017; Bjerregaard et al., 2006). This provides essential context for the experimental work.

results.result: Syncytin-1 and syncytin-2 are expressed in multiple cell lines tested, with syncytin-2 showing more apparent furin processing than syncytin-1, and MDA-MB-231 cells having lower syncytin-1 levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C63 characterize baseline syncytin expression using immunoblotting. The observation of differential processing (C62) is based on protein mobility patterns, which is a reasonable inference but could benefit from direct furin inhibition experiments. The lower syncytin-1 in MDA-MB-231 (C63) is clearly shown in the immunoblot data.

results.result: Syncytin-2 knockdown in MDA-MB-231 acceptor cells dramatically reduces Cas9 transfer, with syncytin-1 knockdown having a smaller effect, and mouse syncytin-A partially rescuing the knockdown phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 and C96 demonstrate syncytin requirement using CRISPRi knockdown. The differential effects of syncytin-1 versus syncytin-2 (C65) suggest syncytin-2 is more important in this system. The rescue by mouse syncytin-A (C66) provides strong evidence for functional conservation and specificity. The controls for dCas9 expression levels are appropriate (described in methods and Figure 7 supplement).

results.result: Full-length syncytin-A rescues Cas9 transfer in syncytin-depleted cells, while truncated versions fail to rescue and act as dominant negatives, demonstrating that intact syncytin structure is required for fusion activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C68 and C97-C98 use structure-function analysis to demonstrate domain requirements. The rescue by full-length but not truncated syncytin-A (C67, C97) supports functional specificity. The dominant-negative effect of truncations (C68) suggests they may interfere with endogenous syncytin function, providing additional mechanistic insight. The multiple truncations tested strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: Syncytin depletion in HEK293T donor cells has a modest effect (~30% reduction) on Cas9 transfer, much smaller than the effect of syncytin-2 depletion in MDA-MB-231 acceptor cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 demonstrate cell-type-specific syncytin requirements. The smaller effect in HEK293T donors (C69) versus MDA-MB-231 acceptors (C65) suggests the acceptor cell syncytin is more critical. This asymmetry is important for understanding the mechanism and is well-supported by the comparative data.

results.result: Ectopic expression of syncytin-A in HEK293T acceptor cells partially enables Cas9 transfer from HEK293T donors (4-fold increase), though less effectively than with MDA-MB-231 acceptors (30-fold), suggesting functional syncytin is limiting in HEK293T cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C73 provide gain-of-function evidence that syncytin-A can partially rescue the HEK293T-HEK293T transfer defect. The modest effect (C72) compared to MDA-MB-231 acceptors suggests additional factors may be limiting in HEK293T cells. The inference that functional syncytin is limited in HEK293T (C73) is reasonable but could reflect other differences (receptor levels, trafficking, etc.).

results.result: Syncytin-2 knockdown in MDA-MB-231 cells prevents formation of open-ended tubular connections with HEK293T cells, with only 1 open-ended connection found in 120 contacts versus 8/120 in control cells, demonstrating that syncytin-2 is required for membrane fusion at tubule-cell junctions.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C77 provide critical structural validation of the syncytin requirement. Live-cell imaging (C74) and CLEM (C75) show persistent close-ended connections with syncytin-2 knockdown. The quantification (C76: 1/120 vs 8/120 in controls) directly links syncytin-2 to membrane fusion. This is the strongest evidence that syncytin-2 mediates the fusion event required for cargo transfer.

results.result: GFP-tagged syncytins localize primarily to intracellular compartments with some surface expression, and cell surface biotinylation detects both precursor and furin-processed forms at the plasma membrane, though most syncytin remains in the secretory pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C83 characterize syncytin trafficking and localization. Immunofluorescence (C78, C81) shows reticular patterns and some surface localization. Biotinylation (C79) confirms surface exposure of processed forms. The interpretation that most protein is in the secretory pathway (C80, C83) is reasonable based on the predominance of full-length protein in total lysates versus processed forms at the surface. The localization to cell-cell junctions (C81) is particularly relevant.

results.result: MFSD2A (syncytin-2 receptor) knockdown reduces Cas9 transfer in both HEK293T donor cells (5-6 fold reduction) and MDA-MB-231 acceptor cells (3-4 fold reduction), indicating MFSD2A plays roles in both cell types and may mediate transfer among MDA-MB-231 cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C87 demonstrate receptor requirement using siRNA knockdown. The effects in both donor and acceptor cells (C84-C85) suggest MFSD2A functions bidirectionally, consistent with its role as syncytin-2 receptor. The inference about MDA-MB-231 to MDA-MB-231 transfer (C87) is reasonable given the earlier observation of self-transfer (C26). However, the mechanism by which receptor knockdown in donor cells affects transfer could be better explained.

results.result: MFSD2A localizes to the cell surface in both endogenous and GFP-tagged forms.
results.evaluation: Claim C88 demonstrates appropriate localization of the syncytin-2 receptor using immunofluorescence. This is important for establishing that MFSD2A is positioned to interact with syncytin-2 at sites of cell-cell contact. The data are straightforward and well-supported by the imaging.

results.result: Syncytin serves as the fusogen responsible for formation of open-ended connections between cells that enable intercellular cargo transfer.
results.evaluation: Claim C100 synthesizes the major findings into a mechanistic model. This conclusion is well-supported by converging evidence: syncytin-2 knockdown blocks both functional transfer (C64-C65) and open-ended connection formation (C74-C77), syncytin-A rescues transfer (C66-C67), and the receptor MFSD2A is required (C84-C87). The model integrates structural and functional data effectively.
